cards.front: The 4 domains of AF management are [___], rhythm control, anticoagulation, and treat reversible causes.
cards.context:
AF management has 4 domains

1. Rate control — target HR <110 (beta-blockers, CCBs, digoxin); first-line if >48h or unknown onset.

2. Rhythm control — cardioversion (electrical or pharmacological with amiodarone/flecainide); consider if symptomatic, young, first episode.

cards.front: The minimum possible GCS score is [___] and maximum is 15.
cards.context: GCS 3 is the minimum (E1V1M1). GCS 15 is the maximum (E4V5M6).

cards.front: Respiratory acidosis HCO₃⁻ compensation: acute = 1 mmol/L per 10 mmHg pCO₂ rise. Chronic = [___] per 10 mmHg.
cards.context:
Acute compensation is minimal (just buffering) because kidneys haven't had time to retain bicarbonate. Chronic compensation (days to weeks) allows kidneys to retain significant bicarbonate, partially normalising pH.

Example: COPD patient with pCO₂ 70 (up 30) → HCO₃⁻ rises ~12 to 36.

cards.front: Secondary hyperalgesia (pain spread beyond injury site) is caused by [___], which is the target of amitriptyline, duloxetine, and gabapentin.
cards.context: Peripheral sensitisation causes hyperalgesia at the injury site only.

cards.front: To replace 2 L intravascular volume with crystalloid (25% retention): 2 ÷ 0.25 = [___] needed.
cards.context:
Isotonic crystalloid distributes across the entire extracellular space, not just intravascular. ~¼ stays in vessels; the rest leaks into interstitium within an hour.

This arithmetic is why crystalloid-only resus in haemorrhage worsens the lethal triad (dilutes clotting factors, drops temperature, drives acidosis with chloride load). Switch to 1:1:1 blood products early.

cards.front: Holliday-Segar daily electrolyte requirements: Na+ is [___] mmol per 100 mL of water, and K+ is 2 mmol per 100 mL.
cards.context:
Daily electrolyte requirements per Holliday-Segar: Na+ = 3 mmol per 100 mL of water requirement. K+ = 2 mmol per 100 mL.

For 70 kg: water = 2500 mL (25 units of 100 mL), so Na+ = 75 mmol/day, K+ = 50 mmol/day.

cards.front: In septic shock after adequate fluid resuscitation (≥30 mL/kg), the next step is starting a [___] infusion.
cards.context:
After adequate fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg, approximately 2.1 L for a 70 kg patient), the next step in septic shock is vasopressor (noradrenaline) — not more fluids.

This follows SSC 2021 Figure 2.

cards.front: Key damage control resuscitation targets: pH greater than 7.2, lactate less than [___] mmol/L, ionised calcium greater than 1.1 mmol/L, and temperature greater than 35°C.
cards.context:
Resuscitation targets during damage control provide specific endpoints to guide product replacement. These numbers should be checked every 30-60 minutes during active MTP.

TBI patients have higher targets because the injured brain tolerates coagulopathy and anaemia poorly.

cards.front: Refractory shock: noradrenaline >0.2-0.3 mcg/kg/min. Add [___] and hydrocortisone, reassess for missed pathology.
cards.context: Rising vasopressor doses signal either inadequate source control, ongoing losses, or refractory vasodilation.

cards.front: CRP above [___] suggests an inflammatory process.
cards.context:
CRP (C-reactive protein) is an acute-phase reactant produced by the liver in response to IL-6. Rises within 6-12 h, peaks at 48-72 h, half-life ~19 h — so trends inform diagnosis and resolution.

Limitations: not specific for infection (also rises in malignancy, autoimmune disease, MI, post-surgery), and lags clinical response by 24-48 h.

cards.front: Dual antiplatelet therapy after TIA is indicated when ABCD² score is ≥ 4; the loading dose of aspirin is [___] mg.
cards.context:
ABCD² ≥4 = high early-stroke-risk TIA. Add clopidogrel to aspirin for 21 days (CHANCE / POINT trials) — DAPT reduces 90-day stroke risk by ~30% compared with aspirin alone.

ABCD² components: Age ≥60 (1), BP ≥140/90 (1), Clinical (unilateral weakness 2 / speech 1 / other 0), Duration (≥60 min 2 / 10-59 1), Diabetes (1).

cards.front: NAC anaphylactoid reactions are infusion-[___]-dependent (not true allergy). Management: stop NAC, give antihistamine, then recommence at a slower infusion.
cards.context:
NAC commonly causes flushing, urticaria, wheeze, or hypotension during the loading dose — but this is an anaphylactoid reaction (direct mast cell degranulation), not true IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.

Management: stop infusion, antihistamine (+ bronchodilator if wheezing), wait for settling, restart same NAC at slower rate. Don't switch agents or label 'allergic to NAC' — no equivalent paracetamol antidote.

cards.front: Wake-up strokes with unknown onset may qualify for thrombectomy up to 24 hours if [___] imaging shows mismatch.
cards.context:
DAWN (NEJM 2018) and DEFUSE-3 (NEJM 2018) extended the thrombectomy window to 24 hours from last-known-well in patients with proximal large-vessel occlusion AND a favourable imagin.

This transformed wake-up strokes from 'too late' to potentially treatable.

cards.front: First-line treatment for anaphylaxis is [___] adrenaline 0.5 mg into the anterolateral thigh.
cards.context:
Anaphylaxis is histamine-driven distributive shock + airway oedema + bronchoconstriction — kills via airway loss or CV collapse within minutes.

IM lateral thigh gives faster, more reliable absorption than deltoid, avoiding IV-bolus risks. Dose 0.5 mg adult, 0.01 mg/kg paediatric (max 0.5), repeat q5min.

cards.front: In TBI, target PaCO₂ is [___] mmHg. Hyperventilation below PaCO₂ 30 causes cerebral vasoconstriction severe enough to worsen ischaemia.
cards.context: Hyperventilation to PaCO₂ below 30 causes severe cerebral vasoconstriction — this can worsen ischaemia in already-injured brain tissue.

cards.front: Digoxin Fab indications: life-threatening arrhythmias or hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >[___] mmol/L).
cards.context:
Digoxin blocks Na/K-ATPase pumps → intracellular sodium rises → cardiac arrhythmias. Extracellular potassium also rises (pump failure) → hyperkalaemia.

Both are indications for urgent Fab.

cards.front: Abdominal compartment syndrome: bladder IAP >[___] mmHg + new organ dysfunction. Shock type: obstructive (compresses IVC).
cards.context:
Mechanism: rising intra-abdominal pressure compresses IVC → ↓ venous return → obstructive shock (like tamponade or massive PE).

Multi-system failure: oliguria, ↑ airway pressures (splinted diaphragm), gut ischaemia.

Trigger is bladder pressure, not waiting for the textbook tense abdomen.

cards.front: Paediatric fluid resuscitation for shock: 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus given rapidly over [___] minutes.
cards.context:
Paediatric shock fluid resuscitation: 20 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid (Hartmann's or 0.9% saline) given over 5-10 minutes per bolus. Reassess after each bolus — heart rate, capillary refill, mental status, urine output.

Children compensate longer than adults via tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction, then crash suddenly — by the time hypotension appears, they've lost 30-40% of circulating volume.

cards.front: Maximum IV phenytoin infusion rate is [___] mg/min to avoid cardiac toxicity.
cards.context:
IV phenytoin must be infused at ≤50 mg/min in adults (≤25 mg/min in elderly or cardiac disease) — faster rates cause hypotension, bradycardia, and asystole. The propylene glycol diluent is itself cardiotoxic.

For a 1 g loading dose, that means at least 20 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring.

cards.front: HFNO delivers flow rates up to 60 L/min and generates [___] cmH2O of CPAP effect.
cards.context:
HFNO delivers gas at 20-60 L/min — matching or exceeding peak inspiratory flow rates so the patient breathes only the delivered gas mixture (no room air entrainment). FiO2 can be set anywhere from 21-100%.

The high flow also generates a small amount of CPAP (2-5 cmH2O), stents the upper airway open, washes out nasopharyngeal dead space, and improves comfort through humidification and warming.

cards.front: Lactate clearance target: >10% in [___] hours. A falling lactate confirms adequate resuscitation (trend matters more than single value).
cards.context: Static lactate snapshots miss the trend. A patient with lactate 6→4 (33% clearance) is resuscitating well; lactate 3→2.8 (7% clearance) suggests ongoing hypoperfusion despite lower absolute value.

cards.front: Three IV fluid intents: [___] (boluses for shock), replacement (match GI/drain losses), and maintenance (daily needs, low-sodium).
cards.context:
Always ask WHY you're prescribing fluid.

Wrong intent = wrong fluid.

cards.front: The initial treatment for malignant hyperthermia is dantrolene at [___] mg/kg IV.
cards.context:
Dantrolene blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (RYR1 receptor) — directly stopping the runaway calcium-driven hypermetabolic cascade. 2.5 mg/kg bolus.

Mortality dropped from >70% pre-dantrolene to <5% with prompt dantrolene. Every theatre must have it stocked.

cards.front: After a significant overdose of an analgesic that targets COX but has a narrow hepatic-safety margin, management includes: check [___] levels at 4 hours, start NAC if indicated by the nomogram, and arrange psychiatric review before discharge.
cards.context:
Paracetamol overdose looks deceptively boring in the first 24 h — nausea, vague abdominal discomfort, normal observations and LFTs. Hepatic injury declares itself at 24-72 h, often after the patient has been discharged.

Protocol: plot serum paracetamol drawn at 4+ h post-ingestion (earlier values can't be interpreted) on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram; above the line.

cards.front: NGT placement is confirmed by aspirate pH ≤[___].
cards.context: The whoosh test has been implicated in multiple patient deaths where feed was administered into the lung. pH ≤5.5 is the gold standard bedside test for gastric placement.
